messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

At thirty-four, Samir, a single American of Lebanese descent, spent a month fighting for his life when a severe bowel obstruction forced him into emergency surgery and a prolonged ICU stay. He still felt the ghost of that sterile air whenever a new scent crossed his path, and months later, a specific moment in his salon cracked his composure. When a long-time client asked for a quick scalp examination before a trim, that medical procedure acted as a trigger, instantly pulling Samir into a flashback complete with the sharp, antiseptic smell he remembered from the operating theater. That olfactory recall bypassed his mind and settled in his chest, triggering a wave of horror and a sudden spike in his heart rate. His body immediately braced for impact, every muscle locking in preparation for danger, because the trigger had hijacked his nervous system. Waking from a nightmare that same week left him sweating and shaking, and the lingering physiological residue acted as a trigger that carried with it the full physical pain in his lower abdomen, flooding him with fresh fear. What frightened Samir most was not the initial jolt, but what followed. The trigger had convinced him he could no longer trust his body, viewing his racing pulse and trembling hands as proof that his physiology had turned against him. That appraisal did not sit quietly. As he grew convinced that these reactions meant he was losing his grip on reality, the constant tension in his shoulders and jaw tightened further, his nervous system bracing for another collapse. The fear of going crazy became a self-reinforcing loop, amplifying the very symptoms that terrified him. His body felt like an untrustworthy machine, sounding alarms long after he was safe, and that very belief made him hyper-vigilant to potential reminders. He stopped scrolling through client photos on his work phone, knowing that his distrust had turned every image into a minefield that would pull him straight back into the memory of the ward. The salon, once the center of his world, became a space of calculated avoidance. Samir began declining clients who showed signs of fatigue or discomfort, citing “scheduling conflicts” instead of admitting that a routine medical procedure felt like a death sentence. His stylist chair stood empty for weeks, and the steady rhythm of his livelihood frayed into isolation. He spent his days scanning the cutting room floor for anyone who looked unwell, because his appraisal that his body was an enemy forced him to treat every ordinary interaction as a potential threat. When the memory’s sudden return made him avoid the very places that sparked it, he simply stopped going to work altogether, leaving his tools gathering dust in a locked drawer. The alertness he carried from the morning would prime the memory to return again, locking him in a cycle he could no longer step out of. Now thirty-eight, Samir walks into therapy carrying the weight of a man who has spent years fighting a war inside his own skin. He seeks help because the avoidance has left him unemployed and financially anxious, but what truly pushes him through the door is the terror that his body will never stop betraying him. He hopes to find a way to quiet the constant alertness and trust himself again, even though he is most afraid that he is already too fractured to ever feel safe in his own head.
